question: How do you decide whether a piece of art is actually good, and not just something you personally like?
lookingFor: A reasoned framework for judging craft and intent separately from personal taste, not a vague 'I just know'.

bullets: Separate personal preference from an assessment of intent and execution
Name concrete criteria such as technical control, coherence of concept, and how well the work does what it sets out to do
Give an example of liking a piece less while still recognising its quality
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I try to ask what the piece is trying to do before I ask whether I enjoyed it, because those are different questions. For me quality is about whether the technical choices actually serve the idea, so a rough, unfinished-looking painting can be more successful than a polished one if the roughness is doing work. A good example is Francis Bacon's distorted portraits, which I find genuinely unsettling to look at, but I still think they are extraordinary because every smear of paint is controlled and deliberate. So I judge on coherence between intention and execution first, and let my own taste sit separately.

commonMistakes: Collapsing quality entirely into personal taste
Reciting 'skill equals good art' with no room for concept-driven work
Refusing to commit to any criteria at all
followUps: Can a technically weak piece still be a great work of art? Why?

question: Which artist has influenced your work the most, and how do you make sure your own work isn't just an imitation of theirs?
lookingFor: Genuine, specific engagement with an influence plus honest reflection on developing a distinct voice.

bullets: Name a specific artist and what exactly is borrowed, technique, subject, or attitude
Show awareness of where imitation ends and personal voice begins
Give a concrete example of departing from the influence in your own work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Peter Doig has shaped how I think about colour and memory, especially the way he lets a landscape feel half remembered rather than observed. When I started painting my grandmother's village I noticed I was copying his palette almost exactly, so I forced myself to work from my own photographs instead of his compositions and to use materials he never touches, like household gloss paint. It still carries his fingerprints but the subject and texture are mine now. I think every young artist starts as an imitator, the work is in noticing it and pushing past it.

commonMistakes: Naming an influence with no specific insight into their work
Claiming total originality with no acknowledged influences
Not distinguishing homage from unconscious copying
followUps: What would you say to a critic who called your work derivative?

question: AI image generators can now produce polished images from a text prompt. Does that count as art, and does it threaten what you're training to do?
lookingFor: An informed, non-panicked take that distinguishes image output from artistic authorship and process.

bullets: Show awareness of how these tools actually work, trained on existing images, prompted rather than made by hand
Distinguish producing an image from the practice of making art, intention, decision-making, embodied process
Give a considered view rather than dismissing the technology outright or overstating the threat
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think the images can be visually impressive, but I'm cautious about calling the process art in the same sense as painting or sculpture, because the thousands of small decisions an artist makes while a piece resists them are what I think the practice actually is. A prompt is closer to art direction than authorship. I don't feel threatened by it exactly, I think it will push hand-based practice to be more explicit about why the physical process matters, the same way photography forced painting to stop being just about representation. I'm more interested in how artists might use these tools as one material among many rather than treating them as a replacement.

commonMistakes: Dismissing AI art entirely without engaging with the actual debate
Having no informed opinion or awareness of the technology
Panicking about job loss rather than discussing artistic authorship
followUps: Would you ever use an AI tool as part of your own practice?

question: The NFT art boom rose and then crashed hard. What did that episode reveal about how value gets assigned to art?
lookingFor: Awareness of the NFT episode and its implications for the art market, not just a snap opinion on whether it was a scam.

bullets: Show basic awareness of what happened, rapid speculative rise followed by a steep drop in prices and trading volume
Separate the speculative, financial side of the boom from any genuine artistic experimentation that happened within it
Draw a broader point about how scarcity, hype, and community can inflate value detached from the work itself
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: What struck me about the NFT boom was how little the conversation was actually about the images, it was mostly about scarcity and speculation, people buying a token as an investment rather than responding to the work. When the market crashed it exposed that a lot of the value was social and financial rather than aesthetic. I don't think that makes every NFT artist a fraud, some genuinely used the format to experiment with ownership and community in interesting ways, but it was a sharp reminder that hype can attach itself to almost any object. It made me think harder about how much of the traditional art market runs on similar dynamics, just slower and with more polish.

commonMistakes: No actual knowledge of what NFTs or the crash involved
Dismissing the whole episode as a joke with no nuance
Missing the chance to connect it to the traditional art market
followUps: Do you think digital-only work will ever be valued the same as physical work?

question: An artist builds their career on painting from other photographers' images without permission or credit, and it becomes hugely successful. Is that acceptable?
lookingFor: Structured ethical reasoning about appropriation, transformation, and credit, not a flat yes or no.

bullets: Acknowledge that appropriation has a real tradition in art but isn't automatically ethical because of that history
Weigh how much the work transforms the source versus simply reproducing it
Land on a position that credit and transformation both matter, rather than refusing to judge
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Appropriation has a long history in art, from Warhol to Richard Prince, so I don't think using someone else's photograph is automatically wrong. But I think the ethics depend on how much the artist actually transforms it and whether they acknowledge the source, because there's a real difference between commenting on an image and just tracing it for profit. If the painting adds a genuinely new idea, a new context, a new meaning, I'm more comfortable with it, but success alone doesn't excuse taking someone's labour without credit. I'd want to know the photographer had at least been asked or acknowledged, even if legally the artist doesn't have to.

commonMistakes: Treating all appropriation as automatically theft
Treating all appropriation as automatically fine because of precedent
Not distinguishing transformation from straightforward copying
followUps: Does it matter if the original photographer was never paid or credited?

question: A student exhibition includes a piece that several classmates find genuinely offensive. The artist says removing it would be censorship. As a member of the committee deciding, what do you do?
lookingFor: Structured ethical reasoning weighing artistic freedom against harm, not a snap verdict either way.

bullets: Take both the artist's freedom and the classmates' objection seriously rather than dismissing either
Distinguish work that provokes or challenges from work that targets or demeans a group
Propose a process, conversation with the artist, context or framing, rather than a unilateral removal or refusal
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd want to actually look closely at what the piece is doing before deciding anything, because provoking discomfort and genuinely demeaning a group aren't the same thing, even though they can look similar from outside. I'd talk to the artist about their intention and to the classmates about specifically what landed badly, because sometimes a label or short statement of context resolves it without removing the work at all. If the piece is targeting people rather than challenging an idea, I think the committee has a responsibility to say no, that isn't the same as censoring art, it's setting a boundary. I don't think freedom of expression means freedom from any consequence or conversation about impact.

commonMistakes: Siding with 'anything goes' with no consideration of harm
Siding with removal immediately with no process or conversation
Refusing to distinguish provocation from targeting a group
followUps: Does your answer change if the piece targets a specific classmate rather than a general group?

question: A gallery offers to represent you, but only if you keep producing a series that sells well, even though you feel you've said everything you want to say with it. What do you do?
lookingFor: A grounded, realistic answer that weighs opportunity against creative integrity, not naive idealism.

bullets: Acknowledge the real value of the opportunity and financial stability rather than dismissing it
Explain what would be lost creatively by continuing a series that feels exhausted
Propose a concrete way to negotiate or compromise rather than an all-or-nothing choice
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I wouldn't want to turn the offer down out of hand, because representation and a stable income are genuinely rare and I know plenty of artists never get that chance. But if I keep making the same series after the ideas have run out I think the work gets hollow and that shows, so I'd try to negotiate, maybe agreeing to finish out a smaller run of the series while pitching the gallery on where I want to take the next body of work. If they weren't willing to make any room for that at all, I'd have a hard conversation with myself about whether the relationship is actually sustainable for my practice long term. I'd rather grow slower with room to develop than get stuck repeating myself.

commonMistakes: Refusing any compromise and treating the offer as pure selling out
Accepting without any reservation about creative cost
Giving no concrete plan, only vague idealism
followUps: How would you know when a series has actually run its course?

question: In a crit, your tutor tells you the project you've spent months on and care deeply about simply isn't working, and suggests you scrap it and start again with weeks left before a deadline. How do you respond?
lookingFor: Maturity in receiving hard critique, ability to separate ego from evaluation, and a clear-headed plan under pressure.

bullets: Show you can take the critique seriously without either collapsing or dismissing it defensively
Ask what specifically isn't working rather than accepting or rejecting the verdict wholesale
Describe a realistic plan for the time left, salvage, pivot, or restart, based on that specific feedback
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first reaction would be to feel pretty defensive, months of work is hard to hear dismissed, but I'd try to sit with that for a moment rather than argue back immediately. I'd ask my tutor to be specific about what isn't landing, whether it's the concept, the execution, or how it reads to someone outside my head, because that tells me whether I need to start over or just rework the presentation. If the core idea is sound but the execution is off, I'd rather fix and refine in the time left than throw everything away. If they're right that the concept itself doesn't hold up, though, I'd rather know that now with weeks to pivot than find out at the final show.

commonMistakes: Getting defensive and dismissing the critique outright
Agreeing instantly with no attempt to understand the specific reasoning
Having no realistic plan for the remaining time
followUps: How do you usually tell the difference between critique worth acting on and critique that isn't?

question: Major museums are under growing pressure to return contested objects, like the Parthenon Marbles or Benin Bronzes, to their countries of origin. Where do you stand on this?
lookingFor: Informed awareness of the debate and a reasoned position that weighs access, ownership, and colonial history.

bullets: Show awareness of at least one real case and the history behind how the objects left their country of origin
Weigh the argument for universal access and preservation against the argument for restitution and cultural ownership
Land on a considered position rather than refusing to engage
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've read about the Benin Bronzes case, where thousands of objects were looted by British forces in 1897 and ended up scattered across museums in Europe and America, and I think that history is hard to separate from any argument about universal access. Museums often say these objects are safer or seen by more people where they are, but that argument feels weaker to me when the original removal was violent and non-consensual rather than a purchase or gift. I lean toward restitution in cases where the origin was clearly looting, though I do think there's a real conversation to be had about loans, shared custodianship, and how objects get cared for once returned. It's not a simple issue and I don't think either side has a monopoly on good intentions.

commonMistakes: No actual knowledge of a real case or the history involved
Taking a flat position with no acknowledgment of the counterargument
Treating it as a purely legal question with no ethical dimension
followUps: Does your view change for objects acquired through purchase rather than looting?

question: Walk me through how you use colour or composition deliberately in one of your recent pieces, not just what looks nice but why.
lookingFor: Ability to articulate deliberate formal decisions and connect them to meaning, not just describe aesthetic preference.

bullets: Reference a specific piece and a specific formal choice, colour palette, framing, balance
Explain the reasoning, what the choice does to the viewer's eye or the work's meaning
Show awareness of an alternative that was rejected and why
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: In a self portrait series I made this year I kept the palette almost entirely desaturated except for one small area of red in each piece, usually somewhere unexpected like a fingernail or a shadow. I wanted the eye to land there first and then have to work its way back out to the rest of the image, which felt like a way of controlling attention the way memory does, one detail sharp and everything else faded. I tried it first with a fuller colour range and it just felt flat, nothing was directing the viewer anywhere, so stripping it back was what actually made the idea legible. It's a small decision but it changed how the whole series reads.

commonMistakes: Describing choices purely in terms of what looks nice
Vague generalities with no specific piece referenced
No mention of an alternative that was considered and rejected
followUps: How do you know when a formal choice is working versus just decorative?

question: Some contemporary artists argue the process of making a work matters more than the finished object. Do you agree?
lookingFor: A considered position on process versus product, grounded in real examples and personal practice.

bullets: Reference at least one artist or movement where process is central, performance art, land art, durational work
Weigh the argument against traditional emphasis on a finished, exhibitable object
Connect the question to your own practice with a concrete example
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think about Ana Mendieta's earth-body works a lot, where the piece existed for a short time and what remains is mostly photographic documentation, which makes the actual making the real artwork rather than any object left behind. I don't think that's true for all art though, a lot of what I love, like Rembrandt's late self portraits, is entirely about the resolved object and the decisions frozen into it. In my own practice I keep a working journal of every failed attempt at a piece, and I've started thinking the journal itself might be as interesting as the final painting, so I'm genuinely torn on this rather than landing firmly on one side. I think the honest answer is it depends what the work is trying to say.

commonMistakes: No real examples, just an abstract opinion
Dismissing process art as not real art with no engagement
Failing to connect the question back to their own practice
followUps: Could you imagine making a piece with no lasting object at all?

question: Tell me about a piece you destroyed or abandoned. What made you walk away from it rather than push through?
lookingFor: Honest reflection on a real creative failure and the judgement to recognise when a piece isn't salvageable.

bullets: Describe a genuine abandoned or destroyed piece, not a disguised success story
Explain the specific reasoning behind walking away rather than continuing to push
Show what was learned and carried into later work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I spent about six weeks on a large canvas trying to paint my father's hands from memory, and about two thirds of the way through I realised I was fighting the composition instead of developing it, every fix created two new problems. I eventually painted over it completely, which felt awful at the time because of how much time was in it. But it taught me that some pieces are actually studies in disguise, useful for what they teach you about a subject, not meant to be the final statement, and the painting I made right after, working smaller and faster, turned out to be one of the strongest things in my portfolio. Now I try to notice earlier when I'm forcing something rather than developing it.

commonMistakes: Choosing a story that's secretly a success dressed up as failure
No genuine reasoning for why the piece was abandoned
Stopping at the abandonment with no lesson carried forward
followUps: How do you tell the difference between a piece worth fighting for and one worth abandoning?

question: Do you think an artist can chase commercial success without compromising their work, or is 'selling out' basically inevitable?
lookingFor: A nuanced view on the tension between sustaining a practice financially and maintaining artistic integrity.

bullets: Reject the binary framing, acknowledge both real risk and real counterexamples
Give a specific example of an artist who navigated commercial success without an obvious loss of integrity
Connect the question to their own priorities as a working artist
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think selling out is inevitable, but I do think it's a real risk that takes active management rather than something that just works itself out. KAWS is someone I think about, he moved between fine art and mass commercial collaborations and plenty of critics wrote him off for it, but I think the work stayed conceptually coherent, the commercial reach was almost part of the point about consumer culture rather than a betrayal of it. What worries me more is compromising quietly, softening an idea because it's easier to sell, without even noticing you're doing it. I'd rather be broke and honest for a while than lose track of why I'm making something in the first place, though I know that's easy to say now.

commonMistakes: Treating commercial success as automatically incompatible with integrity
Having no real example to support the position
Sounding naive about the financial realities of being an artist
followUps: Would you ever take on commercial commission work? What would you refuse?

question: You're drawn to a visual tradition, a textile pattern, a religious symbol, or a ceremonial form, from a culture that isn't your own. How do you decide whether it's appropriate to use it in your work?
lookingFor: Thoughtful ethical reasoning about cultural appropriation versus genuine cross-cultural engagement, not a defensive dismissal.

bullets: Acknowledge the real ethical stakes rather than treating the question as oversensitive
Describe concrete steps, research, context, consultation, that would inform the decision
Distinguish surface-level borrowing from work that engages seriously and credits its sources
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd start by asking myself whether I actually understand the meaning and context of the form, or whether I'm drawn to it purely visually, because those lead to very different kinds of work. I'd try to research its history and, where possible, talk to people from that tradition or read work by artists and scholars from within it, rather than relying on what I already assume. If it's a symbol tied to closed religious or ceremonial practice I'd be very cautious about using it decoratively at all, but if it's a broader visual tradition I'd want my use of it to say something specific and credited rather than just borrowing the surface. I think the difference between appropriation and genuine engagement usually comes down to whether you did the work to understand what you're using.

commonMistakes: Dismissing the concern as oversensitive with no engagement
Refusing to ever engage with any culture outside your own, avoiding the question entirely
No concrete process for how the decision would actually be made
followUps: Has a tutor or peer ever pushed back on a choice like this in your own work?

question: A city commissions a public sculpture using taxpayer money, and it turns out deeply controversial, some residents call it ugly and a waste of funds, others defend it as important art. Should public money fund work like this?
lookingFor: Structured reasoning about public accountability versus artistic freedom in publicly funded work.

bullets: Acknowledge the legitimate tension between public accountability and artistic risk-taking
Reference a real or plausible example of public art controversy to ground the reasoning
Propose a workable middle ground, such as community consultation, rather than an absolute answer
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think about Richard Serra's Tilted Arc, which was removed from a New York plaza after huge public backlash even though plenty of critics considered it an important work, and it's a good example of how public art answers to a different set of people than gallery work does. I don't think that means public money should only fund safe, universally liked work, because some of the most important public art has been genuinely divisive at first. But I do think there's a real obligation to consult the community that has to live with the piece every day, not necessarily to give them a veto, but to take the process seriously rather than treating it as purely the artist's or the committee's decision. Controversy alone isn't a reason to reject a piece, but ignoring the public entirely isn't right either.

commonMistakes: Treating any public objection as reason enough to censor the work
Dismissing the public's view entirely in favour of pure artistic freedom
No real example or grounding for the position taken
followUps: Who do you think should have the final say in commissioning decisions like this?

question: Duchamp put a urinal in a gallery over a century ago and artists have been questioning what counts as original ever since. Does the idea of originality still mean anything today?
lookingFor: Genuine engagement with art historical theory and a reasoned personal position, not a memorised definition.

bullets: Show real understanding of what Duchamp's readymades actually challenged, authorship and the role of choice and context
Acknowledge how appropriation art and postmodern theory complicated the idea of a singular original
Offer a personal, reasoned view rather than just summarising the theory
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: What Duchamp actually shifted, I think, was moving originality away from the object itself and toward the decision and the framing, the idea that choosing and recontextualising something could be the creative act. Sherrie Levine took that even further by rephotographing other photographers' work outright, which pushed the question of originality to its limit. I still think originality means something, but I've come to see it less as making something from nothing and more as bringing a genuinely new perspective or relationship to existing material, even material that already exists. So for me the question isn't whether a work is unprecedented, it's whether it's doing something that couldn't be reduced to its sources.

commonMistakes: Reciting the Duchamp story with no real understanding of what it questioned
Concluding originality is meaningless with no further reasoning
No personal position, only historical summary
followUps: Where do you think the line is between homage and plagiarism?

question: A visiting critic looks at your degree show centrepiece and says, in front of the group, that it feels derivative and safe. How do you respond, in the room and afterward?
lookingFor: Composure under public critique and a mature process for evaluating harsh feedback rather than reacting defensively.

bullets: Show composure in the moment rather than either arguing back defensively or collapsing
Describe asking a clarifying question to understand specifically what reads as safe or derivative
Explain what would happen afterward, genuine reflection rather than either dismissal or total capitulation
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: In the moment I'd try not to get defensive, even though it would sting, and I'd ask them to say more, specifically what about it feels safe, because that's more useful to me than the verdict itself. If they can point to something concrete, maybe that I pulled back from a riskier version of the idea somewhere in the process, I'd take that seriously and sit with it rather than dismissing it to protect my ego. But I wouldn't automatically accept it as fact either, one critic's read isn't the final word, so afterward I'd talk it through with a tutor or peer I trust to see if it lands the same way for them. If it turns out several people see the same thing, that tells me something real I need to work on.

commonMistakes: Arguing back defensively in front of the group
Accepting the criticism completely with no independent judgement
Pretending the feedback doesn't sting at all
followUps: Has that actually happened to you? How did you handle it?

question: Some traditionalists argue digital painting isn't 'real' art because it lacks physical material and can be undone with a click. What's your view?
lookingFor: A reasoned position on medium and material that avoids snobbery in either direction.

bullets: Engage seriously with the argument rather than dismissing it as old-fashioned
Identify what actually differs between digital and physical process, and what stays the same
Land on a position grounded in the artist's intention and skill rather than the tool itself
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I understand where that argument comes from, undo is a real difference, there's no equivalent of a mistake you have to live with and work around the way there is in oil or ink. But I don't think that makes the decisions any less real, a digital painter is still making thousands of choices about colour, mark, and composition, the tool has just changed what a mistake costs. I use both, and honestly the discipline of not relying on undo has made me a more decisive digital painter over time. I'd rather judge the work on what it does than gatekeep based on the material it's made from.

commonMistakes: Dismissing digital art without engaging with the actual argument
Dismissing the traditionalist view as simply outdated snobbery
No personal experience or grounded position, only abstract debate
followUps: Do you think a gallery should display digital and traditional work differently?

question: Many traditional art materials, solvents, certain pigments, resins, have real environmental costs. Do you think about that in your own practice?
lookingFor: Honest, specific reflection on material choices and environmental responsibility, not a token gesture.

bullets: Show concrete awareness of at least one material with a real environmental or health cost
Describe an actual choice made or considered in response, not just good intentions
Acknowledge the tension between sustainability and creative freedom honestly
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I switched from oil-based solvents to a low-odour, less toxic alternative last year partly for my own health but also because the runoff from cleaning brushes was going straight down the studio sink. I've also started buying pigments in bulk to cut down on packaging waste, though I'll admit I haven't fully given up cadmium reds, which are genuinely more toxic to produce, because I haven't found a substitute with the same intensity yet. I don't think I'm anywhere near a fully sustainable practice, but I'd rather make deliberate trade-offs than not think about it at all. It's something I expect to keep adjusting as I learn more.

commonMistakes: Claiming a perfectly sustainable practice with no honest trade-offs
No concrete example, only a vague statement of concern
Dismissing the question as irrelevant to art-making
followUps: Would you ever let material sustainability limit an idea you really wanted to make?

question: Street artists like Banksy have made unauthorised public work into a hugely valued art form, while unknown taggers doing similar things get prosecuted. Is that fair?
lookingFor: Critical awareness of the class and fame dynamics in how street art is judged legally and artistically.

bullets: Acknowledge the double standard between celebrated and prosecuted street artists
Explore what factors actually drive the difference, fame, perceived craft, property owner consent after the fact
Offer a considered view on the underlying property and legal questions
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It's clearly not fair in a strict sense, the actual act, painting on property without permission, is often identical, but Banksy gets a wall protected behind perspex and an unknown tagger gets a criminal record. I think what shifts is retrospective consent and market value, once something is recognised as valuable, property owners suddenly want it there, which says more about our relationship to fame and money than about the legality of the act itself. I don't think that means all street art should be legal regardless of consent, property owners have a real interest in what happens to their walls, but I do think the law is applied with a lot of inconsistency that has more to do with who's famous than what actually happened.

commonMistakes: Treating all street art as automatically legitimate regardless of consent
Treating all unauthorised work as simple vandalism with no nuance
Ignoring the class and fame dynamics behind the double standard
followUps: Would you ever make unauthorised public work yourself? Under what conditions?

question: Should an artist feel free to depict experiences, cultures, or identities that aren't their own, or are there stories that aren't theirs to tell?
lookingFor: Nuanced reasoning about representation, empathy, and responsibility, avoiding both a hard no and a careless anything-goes.

bullets: Reject a blanket rule in either direction, avoid both total restriction and total freedom
Distinguish depicting from a distance versus doing the research and building genuine relationships or collaboration
Discuss accountability, how the artist responds if the depiction causes real harm or gets real pushback
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think there's a story that's absolutely off limits, art has always involved imagining lives beyond your own, but I do think the responsibility scales with how much power or distance separates the artist from the subject. If I wanted to depict an experience far from my own, I'd want to actually do the work, research, conversation, maybe direct collaboration with people from that community, rather than relying on assumption or stereotype. I'd also want to genuinely listen if the depiction lands badly rather than defending it purely on the grounds of artistic freedom. I think the difference between empathy and appropriation usually comes down to whether the work was made with people or just about them.

commonMistakes: Declaring any depiction of another identity automatically off limits
Claiming total artistic freedom with no acknowledgment of responsibility
No concrete process for how research or accountability would actually happen
followUps: How would you respond if a community you depicted said your work misrepresented them?

question: Why did you choose the specific medium you work in most, rather than another one that might convey a similar idea?
lookingFor: Deliberate reasoning connecting medium choice to conceptual intent, not just a statement of preference.

bullets: Name the medium specifically and what it physically allows or resists
Connect that physical quality directly to the ideas the artist wants to express
Show awareness of an alternative medium considered and why it was rejected
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I work mostly in charcoal and graphite because the smudging and erasure stay visible in the final piece, you can see the drawing's history even in what looks finished, which matters to me because my work is largely about memory and how it degrades. I tried the same subjects in oil for a while, and while I liked the colour possibilities, the paint's opacity kept covering up exactly the trace I wanted to keep visible. Charcoal also forces a kind of physical looseness, I work standing up with the paper on the wall, that a more precise medium doesn't. The mess and the visible correction are the point, not a flaw to hide.

commonMistakes: Describing medium choice purely as personal preference with no conceptual link
No comparison to an alternative medium considered
Vague, generic answer that could apply to any medium
followUps: Could this same idea work in a completely different medium? Why or why not?

question: If we handed you a blank sheet of paper right now and asked you to make something in the next twenty minutes while we watched, what would you actually do first?
lookingFor: A realistic, specific process under pressure that reveals genuine working habits, not a rehearsed or vague answer.

bullets: Give a concrete, specific first move rather than a vague description of 'getting inspired'
Explain the reasoning behind that starting point, how it connects to their usual process
Show awareness that working under observation changes the process and address that honestly
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Honestly the first thing I'd do is stop trying to think of a perfect idea and just start marking the page, probably quick gestural lines with no plan, because that's genuinely how I break through a blank page in my own studio too. I'd watch for a shape or rhythm that catches my attention in the marks and then start building from that rather than imposing a concept from the outset. I'll admit being watched would make me want to perform confidence I might not fully feel, so I'd try to actually stay honest to my process rather than doing something flashier than what I'd normally do. It probably wouldn't be a finished piece in twenty minutes, but it would be a real starting point.

commonMistakes: A vague answer about 'waiting for inspiration' with no concrete action
Describing a process that doesn't match how they actually work
No acknowledgment that being observed changes the process
followUps: What usually breaks your block when you're stuck in the studio alone?

question: Some museums have sold works from their permanent collections to cover budget shortfalls, which drew sharp criticism from the art world. What's your view on deaccessioning?
lookingFor: Informed engagement with a real institutional debate and a reasoned position on competing obligations.

bullets: Show awareness of what deaccessioning is and why it's controversial, breaking the norm that collections serve the public rather than operating budgets
Weigh institutional survival and access against the erosion of public trust and future donations
Offer a considered position, perhaps conditional, rather than a flat yes or no
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I know a few museums, including some fairly well known ones, have sold works to cover operating costs, and the art world reaction was pretty harsh because the norm has generally been that deaccessioning proceeds should only fund acquiring other art, not payroll or bills. I understand the argument that a museum has to survive to serve the public at all, and closing entirely would be worse for access than losing one painting. But I do worry it sets a precedent where donors stop trusting that gifted work will stay in the public collection, which could do long-term damage that outweighs the short-term fix. I'd want deaccessioning reserved for genuine emergencies with real transparency about the decision, not treated as a routine budget tool.

commonMistakes: No actual knowledge of what deaccessioning is or why it's controversial
Taking an absolute position with no acknowledgment of institutional survival pressures
Missing the donor trust and precedent dimension entirely
followUps: Should there be different rules for a small regional museum versus a major national one?

question: Do you think a piece of art should be able to stand on its own, or is it fair for it to need an artist's statement to be understood?
lookingFor: A considered view on the relationship between visual work and verbal explanation, grounded in personal practice.

bullets: Avoid an absolute position, acknowledge that different kinds of work need different levels of context
Distinguish a statement that adds depth from one that's doing work the image itself should be doing
Reference the artist's own practice and how they use, or resist using, statements
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think every piece needs a statement to work, some of my favourite paintings hit you immediately with no context at all and that's part of their power. But I've also made conceptual pieces, one series was about erased family photographs, where a line of context genuinely opens the work up rather than doing the work's job for it, the viewer can see more once they know what's missing. I try to write my own statements as an invitation rather than an explanation, a way in rather than an instruction manual for what to feel. If a piece can't survive without a paragraph propping it up, I think that's usually a sign the piece itself needs more work, not that the statement is doing something wrong.
